question: This year’s NATO Summit, in which very dangerous decisions were taken to the detriment of ordinary people, took place in Ankara, Türkiye. The Turkish Government quickly put on a show of power, responding to the anti-NATO protests with a brutal crackdown. Dozens were injured and arrested by the Turkish police, who spared neither members of parliament nor journalists from their sights.

In fact, dozens of members of Türkiye’s Communist Party were arrested. In view of the above, can the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy say: 1.
What view does she take of the brutal crackdown on peaceful protesters by Turkish police forces and the fact that people were arrested even inside their homes to be taken into custody?

What view does she take of the calls not to prosecute protesters – both Turkish and foreign nationals – who had been arrested for expressing their opposition to NATO’s plans, which pose a danger to ordinary people?

What view does she take of the unacceptable restriction of the right to demonstrate and protest, which is regularly applied wherever the NATO Summit is organised, in this case in Ankara and throughout Türkiye?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.9.2026) The Commission has reiterated on numerous occasions that citizens’ participation, including through peaceful protest, is essential to the functioning of an open and democratic society.

As regards individuals arrested in connection with demonstrations, the Commission has consistently called for the full respect for due process, access to legal assistance, and an individual assessment of each case on the basis of credible evidence. Peaceful protest must not in itself lead to prosecution or punitive measures.

The Commission recalls that Türkiye, as a candidate country, a member of the Council of Europe and a party to the European Convention on Human Rights, is expected to uphold the highest democratic standards and to ensure an enabling environment in which people can express their opinions freely and without fear of repression.

While the authorities have a duty to ensure public order and safety, any intervention by law enforcement must be strictly proportionate, based on the rule of law, and respectful of human dignity and fundamental freedoms.

As noted in the 2025 enlargement report on Türkiye1, legislation governing the right to assembly and demonstration, along with its practical implementation, remains inconsistent with European standards. The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers had urged the authorities to amend the Law on demonstrations and meetings in line with the case law of the European Court of Human Rights and the Constitutional Court.
